#### Linear Correlation Plot {#sec-eda-linear-correlation-plot}

**Purpose: Detect Changes in Correlation Between Groups**

Linear correlation plots are used to assess whether or not correlations are consistent across groups. That is, if your data is in groups, you may want to know if a single correlation can be used across all the groups or whether separate correlations are required for each group.

Linear correlation plots are often used in conjunction with [linear slope](#sec-eda-linear-slope-plot), linear intercept ([Linear Intercept Plot](#sec-eda-linear-intercept-plot)), and [linear residual standard deviation](#sec-eda-linear-residual-standard-deviation-plot) plots. A linear correlation plot could be generated initially to see if linear fitting would be a fruitful direction. If the correlations are high, this implies it is worthwhile to continue with the linear slope, intercept, and residual standard deviation plots. If the correlations are weak, a different model needs to be pursued.

In some cases, you might not have groups. Instead you may have different data sets and you want to know if the same correlation can be adequately applied to each of the data sets. In this case, simply think of each distinct data set as a group and apply the linear correlation plot as for groups.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: setup-linear-correlation-plot
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)

# HSU12.DAT has a blank line between each of its 15 batches, which
# read_table() reports as a parsing failure (expected 3 columns, got 1)
# for each blank line -- 14 expected warnings for the 14 gaps between
# batches. drop_na() below removes the resulting all-NA rows.
hsu12 <- read_table(
  here::here("datasets", "HSU12.DAT"),
  skip = 25,
  col_names = c("time", "distance", "batch"),
  col_types = "ddd"
) |>
  drop_na()

group_correlations <- hsu12 |>
  group_by(batch) |>
  summarise(correlation = cor(distance, time), .groups = "drop")

overall_correlation <- cor(hsu12$distance, hsu12$time)
```

**Sample Plot**

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-linear-correlation-plot-sample
#| fig-cap: "Linear correlation plot of the HSU12.DAT data set, by batch"
ggplot(group_correlations, aes(batch, correlation)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = overall_correlation, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:15) +
  labs(x = "Batch (group identifier)", y = "Correlation") +
  theme_light()
```

This linear correlation plot of the HSU12.DAT data set shows that the correlations are high for all groups (all are effectively 1, reflecting the near-perfectly linear relationship between elapsed time and distance for the acoustic microscope within each of the 15 batches). This implies that linear fits could provide a good model for each of these groups.

**Definition: Group Correlations Versus Group ID**

Linear correlation plots are formed by:

- Vertical axis: Group correlations
- Horizontal axis: Group identifier

A reference line is plotted at the correlation between the full data sets.

**Questions**

The linear correlation plot can be used to answer the following questions:

1. Are there linear relationships across groups?
2. Are the strength of the linear relationships relatively constant across the groups?

**Importance: Checking Group Homogeneity**

For grouped data, it may be important to know whether the different groups are homogeneous (i.e., similar) or heterogeneous (i.e., different). Linear correlation plots help answer this question in the context of linear fitting.

**Software**

Most general purpose statistical software programs do not support a linear correlation plot. However, if the statistical program can generate correlations over a group, it should be feasible to write a macro to generate this plot.
